analysis.title: "Here We Go Again": Fed's "Original Sin" Means 10Y Yields Are Going To 8%, TS Lombard Warns
key_insights: TS Lombard chief US economist Steven Blitz, in a note titled "Original Sin Redux", argues the rise in 10Y yields is "not done at 6%". He sees 5.75% as the next plateau and 8% as the long-run target, reached over "a few years" with "plenty of zigs and zags".

Blitz's thesis: the original sin of monetary policy is easing before a downturn has fully starved inflation. He says the Fed under Powell eased late last year as hiring fell but profits rose, under pressure from the Administration and people seeking Powell's job.

Blitz says the administration wants Kevin Warsh to run policy with "eyes wide shut" as a new upcycle begins. Warsh "resisted, sort of" with the September hike of 25bps to 3.75%-4.00%, which Blitz thinks should have been 50bps.
Blitz argues the funds rate "means less than it did". Real discipline will come when long-end yields reach levels that "quash equity performance". He says "the quash will come" but has not yet.

Blitz calls 2025 "the recession that wasn't". Private payrolls ex-hospitals were declining after about 22 months of curve inversion, but no contraction in real growth followed because of large fiscal expansion, Fed cuts as profits turned, and tariffs.

Two adages drive the inflation call: profits lead employment and employment leads inflation, and the best year of inflation is the first year of recovery. Blitz says 2026 was the good inflation year. High profits imply faster hiring and higher base inflation in 2027, assuming the equity market cooperates.

The August core PCE print was 0.2% only because an actual 0.247% rounded down, and benchmarking revisions lowered the series. Supercore rose 0.4%, helped by the biggest-ever jump in other services and a record increase in education costs. The 10Y retraced its entire post-PCE rally.

Sentiment lags the recovery. Job sentiment has fallen far more than the rise in unemployment explains. Blitz expects sentiment to flip next year if hiring picks up as profits suggest. Sentiment in Ohio and Texas is lower than when Trump was re-elected, which is a problem for Republicans before the midterms.

The swap spread is the key signal. Investors prefer receiving floating overnight secured rates for 10 years over owning fixed-coupon sovereigns. That trend has run in the US since 2012 and has gone global since Covid, with UK and French swap spreads collapsed and Germany roughly even.

Blitz's model of the US 10Y swap spread, built on the 1M10Y curve and proxies for bank UST holding constraints, shows a fitted line that keeps sloping down. This points to a steadily increased preference for receiving SOFR over holding Treasuries.

Blitz says the supply of sovereign developed-market debt to be rolled is too large, with deficits rising faster than nominal GDP and no central bank buyers. Roughly half a trillion of hyperscaler investment-grade debt this year is about half of total Treasury supply in DV01 terms.

Blitz expects the easy money plus bigger deficits mix to deliver higher inflation and higher yields with each cycle. He says it ends only with political will to cut inflation at the cost of growth. 2029 is the earliest, and he would not count on it.

The key variable is whether higher yields come from real rates or inflation breakevens. So far it has been real rates, which shook stocks without real damage and avoided a dollar buyers' strike. If the move shifts to inflation premiums, stocks do okay and the dollar bear market gets underway.
US net saving rate has been pushed to zero by heavy government borrowing. Blitz concludes "Eventually, we see an 8% 10Y".
What breaks, in Blitz's view, is the market's confidence that inflation returns to 2% and that you are always rewarded trading stocks and bonds from the long side, not a specific asset.

Goldman one-delta desk head Rich Privorostsky said the rates move is "getting too punitive to ignore" even as equities have stayed resilient. Rabobank called Treasury's expanded buyback in August "YCC-light", saying it interrupted the higher-yield, larger-term-premium loop but likely did not break it.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Highest since 2002. Blitz sees 5.75% as next plateau, with 6% not the end and 8% the long-run target.
Next plateau for the 10Y per TS Lombard.
Driven by supply, fiscal deficits and weaker demand for Treasuries relative to swaps.
The Fed hiked 25bps in a unanimous vote. Blitz questions why it was not 50bps and says the funds rate means less than it did.
Rounded down to 0.2%, with benchmarking revisions lowering the series. The 10Y retraced its post-print rally.
Boosted by the biggest-ever jump in other services and a record rise in education costs.
Heavy government borrowing pushed it to zero with no sign of abating, which supports the supply-driven yield view.

risk_factors: Higher yields could quash equity performance once long-end yields reach levels the market cannot absorb.
Political pressure on the Fed to ease before inflation is starved could raise inflation premiums and start a dollar bear market.
Sovereign debt supply, including hyperscaler investment-grade issuance, with no central bank buyers.
The market's confidence that inflation returns to 2% and that long-side trading is always rewarded could break.
Treasury intervention, such as the expanded buyback program, may limit how high yields go. Rabobank says it interrupted but likely did not break the loop.
vol_and_positioning: Swap spreads: investors prefer receiving floating overnight secured rates for 10 years over owning fixed-coupon sovereigns, a trend in the US since 2012 and global since Covid.
UK and French swap spreads have collapsed and Germany's choice is roughly even, which Blitz calls a risk preference rather than a curve issue.
geopolitical: Midterm elections: Blitz says sentiment in Ohio and Texas is lower than when Trump was re-elected, Florida is no better, and Ohio has dropped steadily since the inauguration.
White House and administration pressure (Trump, Bessent, Hassett) on Warsh to ease and keep policy loose.
cross_bank_references: UBS mid-day note: markets have "refocus[ed] on the strength of US growth."
Goldman's Rich Privorostsky: the rates move is "getting too punitive to ignore".

tension_points.bull_case: Rabobank says Treasury's expanded buyback ("YCC-light") interrupted the loop of higher yields, a larger term premium and still higher yields, so Bessent may cap how far yields rise.
tension_points.bear_case: Blitz expects supply, deficits rising faster than nominal GDP and falling demand for Treasuries (swap spreads) to push the 10Y to 5.75% and eventually 8%, with Fed easing before inflation is starved.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A political decision to cut inflation at the expense of growth, which Blitz says is 2029 at the earliest, or Treasury intervention that breaks the term-premium loop.

tension_points.bull_case: Equities have been resilient, per Goldman's Privorostsky, and if the move shifts to inflation premiums, stocks do okay.
tension_points.bear_case: Yields reaching levels that quash equity performance, with the rates move getting too punitive to ignore.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A shift in yield driver from real rates to inflation breakevens would weaken the bearish stock case.
